summary:
ASTRA is a real-time, AI-powered astronaut health monitoring platform built for long-duration space missions. Using simulated ARTEMIS II crew telemetry, it monitors 23 physiological, behavioral, and environmental signals across five risk areas: space radiation, bone and muscle loss, cardiovascular health, behavioral health, and immune system changes.
The system detects anomalies against each astronaut's personal baseline using a robust z-score model (median + MAD), then explains findings in plain language through an AI layer (LLM with an offline fallback). Live data streams every two seconds over Socket.IO.
Astronauts get a personal dashboard with trend charts, alerts, medical tests, and downloadable PDF health reports. Flight surgeons get a mission-wide alarm console with sound alerts, crew risk overview, ACK/ACK-all, and a guidance box for sending category-specific recommendations. Cabin life-support telemetry and real NASA DONKI space-weather (CME) data provide environmental context.
Built with React, Vite, Recharts, Node.js, Express, Socket.IO, PDFKit, and the NASA DONKI API, and deployed on Vercel. ASTRA shows how explainable AI can support earlier detection of crew health decline, reduce flight-surgeon workload, and keep humans safe beyond Earth.
Prototype for demonstration only; not for clinical use.
details:
ASTRA — Project Details

What it does and how it works

ASTRA (AI Space Health Monitoring) is a real-time crew health monitoring platform for long-duration space missions, demonstrated on a simulated ARTEMIS II mission with four astronauts.

The system continuously tracks 23 health signals across five risk categories:

- Space radiation exposure

- Bone and muscle loss

- Cardiovascular health

- Behavioral and mental health

- Immune system changes

It also monitors seven cabin life-support parameters (O₂, CO₂, pressure, humidity, temperature, radiation rate, and O₂ tank level).

How it works:

1. A mission simulator on the Node.js server advances vitals and cabin telemetry every two seconds, including realistic drift, noise, and pre-scripted deterioration patterns for specific crew members.

2. Each new reading is compared against that astronaut's personal baseline using a robust z-score model built on median and median absolute deviation (MAD), combined with normal/warning/critical threshold checks.

3. Signals that deviate are ranked by severity and produce an anomaly score (0–100), a plain-language cause, and a suggested next step.

4. The server pushes the full state to all connected clients over Socket.IO WebSockets, so dashboards update live.

5. Alerts are created, updated in place to avoid duplicates, and automatically resolved when a signal returns to normal.

6. An AI layer converts findings into a calm, human-readable explanation. It uses an LLM (OpenAI GPT-4o-mini) when configured and falls back to a deterministic on-board explainer when offline.

7. Astronauts see a personal dashboard with trend charts, alerts, medical tests, guidance, and PDF reports. Flight surgeons get a mission-wide alarm console with sound alerts, crew risk overview, ACK/ACK-all, and a guidance box.

8. Flight surgeons can send category-specific recommendations that appear instantly in the astronaut's dashboard, closing the communication loop.

9. The Environment panel also pulls real NASA DONKI coronal mass ejection (CME) data from the past seven days and caches it for six hours.

Benefits

- Earlier detection: Personalized baselines catch subtle, crew-specific changes that fixed thresholds miss.

- Less alert fatigue: Alerts are deduplicated, updated in place, and auto-resolved.

- Explainable AI: Every finding includes a cause and a concrete next step, supporting trust and clinical judgment.

- Reduced flight-surgeon workload: Crew-wide risk tiles and a prioritized alarm console enable fast triage.

- Closed-loop care: Guidance flows from surgeon to astronaut and can be marked resolved.

- Resilience: The offline explainer and cached NASA data keep core functionality working during communication gaps.

- Actionable records: One-click PDF reports summarize profile, anomalies, alerts, tests, guidance, and cabin environment.

- Zero-install access: Runs entirely in a browser, no specialized hardware required.

Intended impact

The project demonstrates how explainable AI can support crew health in deep-space missions where medical evacuation is impossible and ground support may be delayed. It aims to:

- Shift monitoring from reactive to predictive, personalized early warning

- Keep humans in control with surgeon-in-the-loop decision support

- Improve crew safety and mission success on long-duration flights

- Provide a foundation for analog missions (HERA, NEEMO), telemedicine, and future multi-mission fleet monitoring

Tools, languages, and software used

Frontend: React 18, Vite, Recharts, Socket.IO client, CSS

Backend: Node.js, Express, Socket.IO, PDFKit

AI: OpenAI GPT-4o-mini API with a local rule-based fallback explainer

Data: NASA DONKI CME API, simulated wearable and medical telemetry

Security: HMAC-SHA256 signed session tokens with 24-hour expiry and role-based access

Tooling/Deployment: Git, GitHub, Vercel (production deployment), npm

Hardware: No custom hardware was required; the system runs in a standard web browser. The data model is designed to represent wearable biometric sensors, point-of-care medical tests, and cabin life-support telemetry, so it can later ingest real IoT/wearable streams.

How the project is creative

- Personal-baseline anomaly detection instead of one-size-fits-all thresholds, reflecting how crew physiology differs.

- Hybrid AI design: an LLM for natural explanations plus a deterministic offline fallback, so the system works even without connectivity.

- Dual-role experience: separate astronaut and flight-surgeon interfaces with different needs and permissions.

- Alarm console with sound and triage: prioritized banners, severity counts, and mute controls make it feel like a real mission medical console.

- NASA space-weather context: real CME data connects solar activity to crew radiation awareness, rather than treating cabin health in isolation.

- Integrated guidance loop: ML findings generate suggested guidance, which surgeons can edit and send, then resolve.

- Simulated realism: scripted deterioration and realistic drift make the demo credible and testable.

Factors considered

- Clinical safety: the system explains and recommends but never diagnoses, with a clear "not for clinical use" disclaimer.

- Alert fatigue: deduplication, severity ranking, and auto-resolution.

- Explainability and trust: every anomaly has a cause, trend, and next step.

- Failure resilience: offline AI fallback, cached NASA data, stale-data handling.

- Security and privacy: signed sessions, role-based access, no secrets committed.

- Latency and scalability: 2-second broadcast cycle, capped history and alert lists, efficient state push.

- Data realism: metric ranges, units, and crew profiles grounded in plausible space-medicine values.

- Accessibility and usability: responsive layouts, clear color-coded severity, readable light theme.

- Mission constraints: communication blackouts, limited crew time, and the need for concise guidance.

- Prototype scope: simulated data and small crew size to keep the demo reliable within hackathon constraints.

This is a prototype simulation built for demonstration and is not intended for clinical use.
